prompt.context: Board Games Co. (BGC) is a small board game distributor in the U.S. As board games like Settlers of Catan and Monopoly have made a resurgence in the marketplace, so has BGC. However, recent financial reports show that BGC's profits have declined over the last three years, and they've hired us to diagnose the issue.
prompt.question: BGC's profits have been declining despite rising sales. What is driving this, and what should BGC do about it?

clarifying_info.q: What does BGC sell and to whom?
clarifying_info.a: BGC sells 5 SKUs to boutique gaming retailers.

clarifying_info.q: How many distribution centers does BGC have and where?
clarifying_info.a: BGC has 3 distribution centers in Georgia, Nevada, and New York.

clarifying_info.q: What are BGC's recent sales and profit figures?
clarifying_info.a: Sales were $20M in 2012, $22M in 2013, and $25M in 2014. Profits were $2.0M in 2012, $1.8M in 2013, and $1.4M in 2014.

exhibits.title: Historical Financials ($M)
exhibits.shows: A table and chart showing BGC's three-year income statement (Sales, COGS, Gross Margin, SG&A, Profit) from 2012 to 2014, alongside a dual-axis graph of Sales ($M) and Profit Margin (%).

exhibits.title: SG&A Historical Financials Deep Dive ($M)
exhibits.shows: A line-item breakdown of SG&A costs across 2012, 2013, and 2014, covering eight expense categories.

exhibits.title: 2014 Forecast, Actual Demand, and Fill Rates
exhibits.shows: A table showing, for each of 5 SKUs, the 2014 forecasted demand, actual demand, and the percentage of orders filled by the primary (closest), secondary, and tertiary distribution center. Notes clarify that primary fill costs $1/item, secondary $2/item, and tertiary $4/item.

framework: Revenue: Assess sales trends (volume, price, mix) — sales are growing, so revenue is not the core issue
COGS / Gross Margin: Check whether cost of goods is rising proportionally with sales
SG&A / Operating Costs: Identify which cost line is growing faster than revenue (the main driver)
Root cause drill-down: Once SG&A is flagged, decompose into sub-categories to isolate the specific line item
Supply chain / operations lens: Investigate fulfillment, inventory allocation, and distribution efficiency
Quantify the opportunity: Calculate potential savings from fixing the identified issue
Recommendation: Propose actionable next steps with trade-off awareness

questions.prompt: What do you observe from Exhibit 1? What is driving the profit decline?
questions.guidance: Sales are rising 10% (2012-2013) and 14% (2013-2014). COGS is rising proportionally — gross margin is healthy and stable at 60%. The problem is SG&A: it rose from $10M to $11.2M (+12%) to $13.6M (+21%), growing faster than sales. Profit margin compressed from 10% to 8% to 6%. The candidate should identify SG&A as the culprit and ask to see a SG&A breakdown.

math.setup: Sales growth and margin trend check
math.answer: SG&A growing faster than sales is the root cause of margin compression.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 2, which SG&A line item is most concerning and why?
questions.guidance: Shipping & Delivery is the outlier: it grew from $2.0M (2012) to $2.5M (2013) to $4.0M (2014) — a 100% increase over two years while sales grew only 25%. All other line items are growing at moderate, reasonable rates. The candidate should zero in on Shipping & Delivery and hypothesize about root causes (e.g., poor inventory placement, low fill rates, more distant shipping).

steps: Sales total growth over same period: (25-20)/20 = 25%
math.answer: Shipping & Delivery doubled while sales grew only 25% — a clear red flag.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, calculate the maximum potential savings BGC could achieve if all orders were shipped from the primary (nearest) distribution center.
questions.guidance: For each SKU, compute secondary units filled and tertiary units filled. Savings per unit: secondary fill costs $1 more than primary ($2-$1); tertiary fill costs $3 more than primary ($4-$1). Multiply units by incremental cost and sum across all SKUs to get total possible savings of ~$1.7M.

math.setup: For each SKU: (Actual Demand x Secondary%) x $1 + (Actual Demand x Tertiary%) x $3 = possible savings
math.answer: Maximum possible savings from achieving 100% primary fill rates = ~$1.7M, which would nearly double 2014 profit from $1.4M to ~$3.1M.

brainstorming.prompt: What are possible root causes for BGC's poor primary fill rates, and what could BGC do to improve inventory allocation across its distribution centers?

categories.name: Inventory Allocation Process
ideas: No demand-based allocation model — inventory split equally across DCs regardless of regional demand
Static allocation that ignores historical sales patterns by geography
No rebalancing mechanism between DCs when one runs low

categories.name: Forecasting & Planning
ideas: Regional demand forecasts not disaggregated to DC level
No SKU-level forecasting by distribution center
Forecast accuracy varies by SKU — Exhibit 3 shows forecasting is actually decent company-wide, but allocation is mismatched

categories.name: Systems & Data
ideas: Lack of real-time inventory visibility across DCs
ERP/WMS system not integrated across all three DCs

categories.name: Structural / Network
ideas: DC locations (Georgia, Nevada, New York) may not be optimally positioned relative to customer concentration
Too few DCs to serve all boutique retailer geographies cost-effectively
Capacity constraints at one DC forcing overflow to further DCs

categories.name: Trade-off Considerations
ideas: Holding more inventory at each DC would improve fill rates but increase holding costs
Rebalancing between DCs incurs transfer costs — need to compare to shipping premium
Safety stock policies may need to be set per-SKU and per-DC

recommendation: BGC is experiencing a profit decline driven entirely by SG&A cost growth, specifically a doubling of Shipping & Delivery costs from $2M to $4M over two years.

The root cause is poor inventory allocation across the three distribution centers — BGC holds the right total inventory but distributes it incorrectly, resulting in low primary fill rates and expensive secondary/tertiary shipments.
BGC should conduct an immediate inventory allocation review: analyze regional demand patterns by SKU, redesign allocation rules, and implement DC-level forecasting to maximize primary fill rates.
Achieving full primary fill would save approximately $1.7M annually, nearly doubling 2014 profit from $1.4M to $3.1M.
risks: Improving primary fill rates by holding more inventory per DC increases inventory holding costs — the net benefit must be validated
Transfer/rebalancing costs between DCs could offset some savings
Customer concentration by region is unknown — a broader DC network study may be needed before committing capital
Implementation complexity: upgrading planning systems and retraining staff takes time and upfront investment
next_steps: Conduct a regional demand analysis by SKU to establish DC-level allocation targets
Evaluate trade-off between inventory rebalancing vs. holding higher safety stock at each DC
Assess whether current three-DC network (GA, NV, NY) is optimally sited relative to boutique retailer geography
Implement a DC-level demand forecasting and inventory management system
Set KPIs for primary fill rate improvement and track monthly
